definition:
The doctrine of the Messiah is the church's confession that Jesus of Nazareth is the one Israel's Scriptures promised: the anointed king from David's line, and more than that, the one in whom all of God's promises to Abraham, to Moses, to David, and through the prophets come true. Paul puts it in a sentence: “For all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (2 Corinthians 1:20). The early Christian message was not first a new religion but a claim about Israel's story: that its long-awaited deliverer had come, had been crucified, and had been raised. This study traces how that hope grew through the Old Testament and how the New Testament reads it in Jesus. Who Jesus is as God and man is the subject of the study on the incarnation; his work as prophet, priest, and king, his atoning death, his resurrection, and his present reign each have their own studies, and the site's page on who Jesus is sets out the church's full Christology.

Messiah is the English form of the Hebrew mashiach, ‘anointed one’, from the verb mashach, ‘to smear or anoint’. In Israel oil was poured on a person set apart by God for a task: above all the king, who is repeatedly called ‘the LORD's anointed’ (1 Samuel 24:6), but also the high priest, “the anointed priest” (Leviticus 4:3), and once a prophet, Elisha (1 Kings 19:16). The noun appears about forty times in the Hebrew Bible, nearly always of a reigning king, and once of the Persian king Cyrus (Isaiah 45:1), whom God had appointed to free the exiles. So the word itself is ordinary; the hope attached to it grew larger than the word. The Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures made in the last centuries before Christ, rendered mashiach with christos, from chriō, ‘to anoint’, and that is the word behind ‘Christ’ in English. It appears more than five hundred times in the New Testament; the Hebrew form transliterated into Greek, Messias, appears only twice, both in John, each time glossed for Greek readers (John 1:41; John 4:25). In the Gospels ‘the Christ’ is a title with a question attached to it, whether this man is the one. In Paul's letters ‘Christ’ often works almost like a name, but it never stops meaning ‘the anointed king’ (Romans 9:5).
ot:
The Old Testament does not present a single, finished portrait of a coming Messiah. It plants promises along the length of Israel's story, and they gather force as the story goes wrong. The first comes in the ruins of the fall. God tells the serpent that the woman's offspring will crush its head while the serpent strikes his heel (Genesis 3:15). The Hebrew zera‘, ‘seed’ or ‘offspring’, can mean a whole line of descendants or one person, and the verse leaves both open; Irenaeus in the second century read it of Christ, and later Christian tradition named it the protevangelium, the ‘first gospel’, while many Jewish and modern interpreters read it as the lasting struggle between humanity and evil. The promise narrows through Abraham, through whom “all the families of the earth will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3), and then through Judah, from whom “The scepter will not depart” (Genesis 49:10). That verse contains a famously difficult phrase, read as a place name (‘until Shiloh comes’) or as ‘until he comes to whom it belongs’; the Aramaic Targum Onkelos already read it of the Messiah. Balaam, a foreign seer, sees “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel” (Numbers 24:17). Moses promises that God will raise up “a prophet like me from among your brothers” (Deuteronomy 18:15), a promise the closing words of Deuteronomy say was not yet fulfilled in Israel's history (Deuteronomy 34:10).

The center of gravity is David. When David was anointed, “the Spirit of the LORD rushed upon David from that day forward” (1 Samuel 16:13), and God later swore by covenant, through the prophet Nathan, to raise up David's descendant, to be his Father, and to establish “the throne of his kingdom forever” (2 Samuel 7:13-14). The royal psalms, sung at the coronations and in the worship of Judah's kings, speak of the king in terms no actual king filled. In Psalm 2 the nations rage “against the LORD and against His Anointed One”, and God says to the king, “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (Psalm 2:2, 7), language drawn from the adoption of the king at his enthronement. Psalm 110 has David's ‘Lord’ seated at God's right hand and made “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (Psalm 110:1, 4), joining kingship and priesthood in one figure. Psalm 89 holds God to his oath to David while lamenting that the crown lies in the dust. That tension, a promise sworn forever and a dynasty that failed, is where messianic hope is born.

As the kingdom divided and fell to Assyria (722 BC) and Babylon (587 or 586 BC), the prophets looked beyond the failed kings to a king God himself would raise. Isaiah speaks of a child on David's throne whose names include “Mighty God” and whose rule has no end (Isaiah 9:6-7), and of “a shoot will spring up from the stump of Jesse” on whom the Spirit rests, who judges the poor with righteousness (Isaiah 11:1-5). Jeremiah promises “a righteous Branch” for David (Jeremiah 23:5); Hebrew tsemach, ‘sprout’ or ‘branch’, became a title for the coming king in Zechariah (Zechariah 3:8; 6:12). Ezekiel promises “one shepherd, My servant David” over a reunited people (Ezekiel 34:23), and Micah a ruler from Bethlehem “whose origins are of old” (Micah 5:2). Zechariah sees Zion's king coming “humble and riding on a donkey” (Zechariah 9:9), a king of peace rather than of chariots.

Two other figures enter the picture, and the Old Testament never explicitly fuses them with the king. In Isaiah 40 to 55 the Servant of the LORD bears God's Spirit and brings justice to the nations (Isaiah 42:1-4), and in the fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12) he is despised, “pierced for our transgressions”, and makes his life a guilt offering, and then “He will see His offspring” (Isaiah 53:5, 10). Whether the Servant is Israel, a faithful remnant, the prophet, or a future individual is debated in the text itself, which calls Israel God's servant (Isaiah 49:3) and also has the Servant restore Israel (Isaiah 49:5-6). In Daniel's vision, written in Aramaic, “One like the Son of Man coming with the clouds of heaven” receives an everlasting kingdom from the Ancient of Days (Daniel 7:13-14); the Aramaic bar ’enash simply means ‘a human being’, a human figure set against the beasts of the empires. Daniel 9:25-26 speaks of an ‘anointed one’ who will be “cut off”, a passage read of Jesus by much of the church and, by many modern scholars, of the high priest Onias III, murdered in about 171 BC. The Old Testament closes with the LORD promising to come suddenly to his temple after a messenger prepares the way (Malachi 3:1). The promised king, the prophet like Moses, the suffering Servant, and the Son of Man stand side by side, unexplained, waiting.
nt:
Between the Testaments, Jewish hope took many forms. The Psalms of Solomon (chapter 17, first century BC) long for a son of David who will purge Jerusalem of the Romans and rule in righteousness. Some of the Dead Sea Scrolls expect two anointed figures, a priestly Messiah of Aaron and a royal Messiah of Israel (1QS 9:11), and one fragment (4Q521) links God's anointed with healing the sick and raising the dead. There was no single agreed script, and most scholars find no clear pre-Christian expectation of a Messiah who would be crucified. That is the setting of the Gospels, where the question “Are You the One who was to come?” (Matthew 11:3) hangs over Jesus' whole ministry. Matthew opens by naming him “Jesus Christ, the son of David, the son of Abraham” (Matthew 1:1), and Luke's angel announces him as “Christ the Lord” born in David's town (Luke 2:11). At his baptism the Spirit descends and the Father's voice joins the royal words of Psalm 2:7 to the Servant of Isaiah 42:1, “You are My beloved Son; in You I am well pleased” (Mark 1:11). In the synagogue at Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61, “He has anointed Me”, and says, “Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luke 4:18, 21). His answer to John the Baptist is a list of deeds drawn from Isaiah (Matthew 11:4-6).

Yet Jesus handles the title with striking reserve. When the crowd wants to “make Him king by force” he withdraws (John 6:15), and when Peter confesses, “You are the Christ”, Jesus tells the disciples to tell no one and immediately teaches “that the Son of Man must suffer many things” (Mark 8:29-31). He prefers to call himself the Son of Man, the figure of Daniel 7, and fills it with the Servant's suffering: “the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). He enters Jerusalem on a donkey as Zechariah foretold (Matthew 21:4-5), asks how David can call his own son ‘Lord’ in Psalm 110 (Matthew 22:41-46), and at his trial, asked whether he is the Christ, answers, “I am”, joining Psalm 110 and Daniel 7 in one sentence (Mark 14:61-62). He is executed under a charge of claiming to be “Christ, a King” (Luke 23:2), and mocked on the cross as “the Christ, the King of Israel” (Mark 15:32). By every expectation of the time, a crucified Messiah was a contradiction. Paul admits that “Christ crucified” is “a stumbling block to Jews” (1 Corinthians 1:23).

The resurrection is what turned the contradiction into the church's message. The risen Jesus tells the two on the Emmaus road, “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” and explains “what was written in all the Scriptures about Himself” (Luke 24:26-27), naming the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms (Luke 24:44). From then on the apostles read the promises together: the king of David's line is the Servant who suffers and the Son of Man who is enthroned. Peter at Pentecost concludes that God “has made this Jesus, whom you crucified, both Lord and Christ” (Acts 2:36), citing Psalm 16 and Psalm 110; Paul in the synagogues argues “that the Christ had to suffer and rise from the dead” (Acts 17:3). Paul's summary of the gospel calls Jesus “a descendant of David according to the flesh” who was “declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (Romans 1:3-4), and he hands on as tradition that “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3). Galatians 3:16 reads the promised ‘seed’ of Abraham as finally one person, Christ, and then includes everyone who belongs to him (Galatians 3:29).

The rest of the New Testament fills out what kind of Messiah this is. Hebrews reads Psalm 110 to show that Jesus is the priest-king in the order of Melchizedek (Hebrews 5:5-10; 7:1-28), and Psalm 45 to address the Son as God (Hebrews 1:8-9). Luke's accounts stress that God anointed Jesus “with the Holy Spirit and with power” (Acts 10:38), so that the title names the Spirit's anointing and not only a royal ceremony. The disciples at Antioch were soon nicknamed Christians, ‘Christ people’ (Acts 11:26). Revelation shows the victor of the Davidic hope as “the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David”, who appears as a slain Lamb (Revelation 5:5-6), and ends with Jesus naming himself “the Root and the Offspring of David” (Revelation 22:16). The kingdom still awaits its fullness, when “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ” (Revelation 11:15). The New Testament's claim is that the Messiah has come, has reigned from a cross, now reigns at God's right hand, and will come again.

keyTexts.why: The offspring of the woman will crush the serpent's head and be struck in the process. Read of Christ since Irenaeus and later named the ‘first gospel’; the promise of victory through wounding runs under the whole story.
Jacob's blessing gives Judah the scepter and the obedience of the nations. The Targums read it of the Messiah; it anchors the hope in the tribe of Judah.
God will raise up a prophet like Moses whom Israel must hear. Peter and Stephen apply it to Jesus (Acts 3:22; 7:37), and John's Gospel echoes it (John 6:14).
God's covenant with David: a son on his throne, God as that son's Father, a kingdom forever. The root of every later hope for a son of David.
The nations rage against the LORD and his anointed, and God declares the king his Son. Echoed at Jesus' baptism and transfiguration and quoted in Acts 4:25-27 and 13:33.
David's Lord sits at God's right hand and is a priest forever like Melchizedek. The Old Testament text the New Testament cites most often.
A child born to David's house whose names include Mighty God, whose peaceful rule on David's throne will never end.
A shoot from Jesse's stump on whom the Spirit rests, who judges the poor in righteousness and brings a peace that reaches the whole creation.
The Servant is despised, pierced for others' transgressions, and exalted. The New Testament's key text for a Messiah who suffers (Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:22-25).
One like a son of man comes with the clouds and receives an everlasting kingdom. The source of Jesus' favorite way of speaking of himself.
Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ, and Jesus at once teaches that the Son of Man must suffer, die, and rise. The hinge of Mark's Gospel.
Asked at his trial whether he is the Christ, Jesus says “I am” and joins Psalm 110 to Daniel 7. The claim for which he was condemned.
The risen Jesus explains that the Christ had to suffer and then enter his glory, beginning with Moses and all the Prophets. The key to how the apostles read the Old Testament.
The gospel promised through the prophets concerns God's Son, David's descendant according to the flesh, declared Son of God in power by the resurrection.
The Lion of Judah and Root of David turns out to be a Lamb that was slain. The messianic hope fulfilled by way of the cross.

history:
The first Christians were Jews arguing from Israel's Scriptures, and the first Christian theology was largely a reading of messianic texts. Justin Martyr's Dialogue with Trypho (about 155 to 160) stages a long debate with a Jewish teacher over whether the prophecies fit a crucified Messiah, and Irenaeus's Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching (late second century) sets out the gospel as the fulfillment of the prophets. Origen, in Against Celsus (about 248), records a Jewish interlocutor who read the Servant of Isaiah 53 as the whole people of Israel, a reading that remains central in Jewish interpretation. Eusebius of Caesarea, in his Church History (early fourth century), observed that Israel anointed prophets, priests, and kings, and that Christ alone was all three, the seed of the later doctrine of the threefold office that John Calvin set out in the Institutes (book 2, chapter 15). Augustine's City of God (book 17) traces the prophecies of Christ from Samuel through the kings and prophets. The creeds took the title into their core: the Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed (325, expanded at Constantinople in 381) confess faith in ‘Jesus Christ’ and ‘one Lord Jesus Christ’, and the Council of Chalcedon (451) defined the one Christ as fully God and fully man. Those questions of his person belong to the study on the incarnation; the point here is that the church never let the Jewish title fall away from his name.

Jewish tradition, meanwhile, developed its own messianic thought. The Aramaic Targum on Isaiah reads Isaiah 52:13 as ‘my servant the Messiah’ while turning the suffering toward the nations. The Babylonian Talmud (Sukkah 52a) speaks of a Messiah son of Joseph who will be slain, alongside the Messiah son of David, connecting the mourning of Zechariah 12:10 with him. During the revolt of 132 to 135 Rabbi Akiva is reported (Jerusalem Talmud, Ta‘anit 4:5) to have applied the star of Numbers 24:17 to the rebel leader Simon bar Kosiba, whose followers called him Bar Kokhba, ‘son of the star’; the revolt's crushing chastened later messianic expectation. Moses Maimonides in the twelfth century made belief in the Messiah's coming one of his thirteen principles of faith, and in his law code (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings, chapters 11 and 12) described the Messiah as a king of David's line who restores Israel's sovereignty, rebuilds the temple, and gathers the exiles. Rashi (died 1105) read Isaiah 53 of Israel. In the Disputation of Barcelona in 1263, held before King James I of Aragon, Nachmanides argued against the convert Pablo Christiani that the Messiah had not come because the world was not yet at peace, the objection Jewish readers have pressed ever since. The episode of Sabbatai Zevi, proclaimed Messiah in 1665 and converted to Islam in 1666, left deep scars on Jewish messianism.

The Reformation argued over how directly the Old Testament speaks of Christ. Luther read the Psalms as the voice of Christ throughout. Calvin more often read the royal psalms first of David and then of Christ, whom David foreshadowed, and the Lutheran Aegidius Hunnius attacked this approach in Calvinus Judaizans (1593), ‘Calvin the Judaizer’. In the modern period, critical scholarship asked whether Jesus ever claimed to be the Messiah. Hermann Samuel Reimarus, in a fragment published by Gotthold Lessing in 1778, argued that Jesus expected to be a political Messiah and that his disciples invented a spiritual one after his failure. William Wrede's The Messianic Secret (1901) argued that Mark's commands to silence were the evangelist's device to explain why a non-messianic life was later confessed as messianic. Albert Schweitzer's The Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) portrayed Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet who believed himself the coming Messiah. Sigmund Mowinckel's He That Cometh (Norwegian 1951, English 1956) traced the growth of the idea from Israel's royal ideology. More recent work, including N. T. Wright's Jesus and the Victory of God (1996), has argued that Jesus deliberately acted out a messianic vocation redefined by suffering. Christian reckoning with its own history has also reshaped the doctrine: the Second Vatican Council's declaration Nostra Aetate (1965) rejected the charge that the Jewish people as a whole bear guilt for Christ's death.

differ.body: Many interpreters, especially in older Protestant and evangelical scholarship, hold that the Old Testament contains direct predictions of the Messiah that were meant and understood as such by their human authors, so that Genesis 3:15, 2 Samuel 7, Isaiah 7:14, Isaiah 53, and Micah 5:2 speak of Christ in their original sense. Ernst Wilhelm Hengstenberg's Christology of the Old Testament (1829 to 1835) is a classic statement, and Walter C. Kaiser Jr.'s The Messiah in the Old Testament (1995) a modern one. Its defenders argue that this is how Jesus and the apostles argued (Luke 24:27; Acts 17:2-3), and that the argument from fulfilled prophecy has force only if the prophecies really pointed forward.

Others hold that many texts the New Testament applies to Jesus were first about a person or event in Israel's history (David's sufferings in Psalm 22, the exodus in Hosea 11:1, the king's enthronement in Psalm 2) and that they point to Christ because God shaped Israel's history into patterns that Christ completes. Calvin often read the royal psalms this way, and Leonhard Goppelt's Typos (1939) gave the approach its modern scholarly form. Its defenders argue that it honors the original setting of each text while explaining why Matthew can say such texts are ‘fulfilled’, and that it protects against reading prophecy as mere puzzle-solving.

Some Catholic and Protestant interpreters speak of a sensus plenior, a ‘fuller sense’ intended by God but not fully grasped by the human author, which later revelation brings to light. Raymond E. Brown's dissertation The Sensus Plenior of Sacred Scripture (1955) is the standard modern treatment. Its defenders argue that this accounts for texts, such as Isaiah 7:14, where the New Testament meaning seems larger than the prophet's immediate horizon, while still grounding that meaning in God's authorship of Scripture rather than in the reader's ingenuity.

A further group of scholars, including Richard B. Hays in Reading Backwards (2014) and Peter Enns, who calls the approach christotelic, holds that the apostles learned to read the Old Testament in light of the crucified and risen Jesus, so that texts took on messianic meaning they did not plainly carry before. Its defenders point to Luke 24:45, where Jesus ‘opened their minds’ to the Scriptures, and argue that this approach is honest about the Jewish reading of the same texts while confessing that the whole story finds its goal in Christ. Critics in the other camps answer that it risks making fulfillment depend on hindsight rather than on God's promise; its defenders reply that promise and hindsight are both God's work.

errors:
The church has rejected two opposite distortions. The first reduces the Messiah to a political deliverer: a king who would drive out Rome, or in later forms a national savior whose cause is identified with one people's power. Jesus refused that crown (John 6:15) and was crucified by those who feared it. Every attempt to conscript the title for a party, a nation, or a revolution, whether in the crusading rhetoric of the Middle Ages or in modern nationalisms, repeats the temptation he turned down. The second distortion severs the Messiah from Israel altogether, as Marcion did in the second century when he rejected the Old Testament and its God, and as some modern theology did when it treated Jesus as a timeless teacher whose Jewishness was incidental. The church answered Marcion by keeping the Old Testament as its Scripture, and the New Testament's title for Jesus is itself a Jewish confession. Jesus is Israel's Messiah before he is anyone else's.

The church must also name its own sin. Christians for centuries used the claim that Jesus is the Messiah as a weapon against Jewish neighbors, from the charge of deicide to forced disputations and expulsions, and Luther's late tract On the Jews and Their Lies (1543) is among the darkest examples. That history is not the doctrine but a betrayal of it, since the Messiah the church confesses is the crucified king who prayed for those who killed him. Finally, false messiahs are a real danger that Jesus himself foretold (Mark 13:21-22). The test the New Testament gives is not charisma or success but the shape of the cross and the confession that the Messiah has come in the flesh (1 John 4:2-3).
life:
To confess Jesus as the Christ is to say that history is not a string of accidents. God made promises, kept them over centuries of failure and exile, and kept them in a way no one expected. That changes how a person waits. The long silences of the Old Testament, the failed kings and the fallen city, were not the end of the story, and neither are the delays and losses of a single life. It also changes what kind of power a Christian trusts. The anointed king of Scripture rules by the Spirit, judges the poor with justice, rides a donkey, and wins through a cross. Those who belong to him are anointed with the same Spirit (2 Corinthians 1:21-22) and are called to the same kind of life: to serve rather than to be served.

It also shapes prayer and hope. The first Christians prayed Psalm 2 when they were threatened (Acts 4:24-30), trusting that the nations' rage against the Lord's anointed had already been answered by the resurrection. The church still prays for the day when the kingdom of the world becomes the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and the Lord's Prayer asks for that kingdom to come. Knowing that Jesus is Israel's Messiah also calls Christians to read the Old Testament as their own Scripture, patiently and in its own setting, and to treat the Jewish people, from whom “proceeds the human descent of Christ” (Romans 9:5), with honor.
questions: The Old Testament's promises about the Messiah come as scattered pieces: a seed, a king, a prophet, a servant, a son of man. Why might God have given the hope in pieces rather than in one clear portrait, and what did the pieces have in common?

Jesus repeatedly told people not to call him the Messiah and spoke instead of the Son of Man who must suffer. What were people expecting, and what did he need to change in their expectation before the title could be used rightly?

The Messiah reigns now from God's right hand, yet the world does not look fully ruled by him. Where do you most feel the gap between the promise and what you see, and how do Psalm 2 and Psalm 110 speak into that gap?
